title: Levers & Mechanical Advantage
summary: Every lever trades force for distance, or distance for force - never both at once.
quick_actions: A lever has three parts: the fulcrum (pivot point), the effort (force applied), and the resistance (the load being moved).
First-class lever: fulcrum is between the effort and the resistance (a seesaw, a crowbar, pliers). Can multiply force or multiply speed/distance, depending on which side of the fulcrum is longer.

Second-class lever: the resistance is between the fulcrum and the effort (a wheelbarrow, a bottle opener, a nutcracker). Always multiplies force - you always have a mechanical advantage greater than 1.

Third-class lever: the effort is between the fulcrum and the resistance (a broom, a fishing rod, your own forearm lifting a weight). Always multiplies speed/distance at the cost of force - you always need more effort than the resistance you're moving.

Mechanical advantage = the ratio of resistance to effort. A machine never creates energy - it only trades force against distance, so a bigger mechanical advantage always means moving your end of the lever farther than the load moves.

diagram.alt: Three diagrams: a simple lever labeled with fulcrum/effort/resistance, the three classes of levers shown side by side with a sailor demonstrating each, and a diagram showing oars as levers with the oarlock as the fulcrum
diagram.caption: Figures 1-1 to 1-3. A simple lever, the three lever classes side by side, and oars as a familiar first-class-lever example.

more_info: A crowbar (first class) and a wheelbarrow (second class) both multiply force, but a fishing rod (third class) multiplies the speed of the tip at the cost of needing more force at your hand than the fish actually pulls back with - that trade-off is the whole point of a third-class lever, not a flaw in it.

title: Pulleys & Block and Tackle
summary: More rope through more pulleys means less force needed - but more rope to pull.
quick_actions: A single fixed pulley changes the direction of a pull (pull down to lift up) but gives no mechanical advantage - the force in equals the force out.
A movable pulley (attached to the load itself) gives a mechanical advantage of 2 - half the force needed, but you pull twice the length of rope.
A block and tackle (multiple pulleys combined) multiplies this further: the mechanical advantage roughly equals the number of rope segments actually supporting the moving block.

The trade-off is always the same as with any simple machine: whatever force you save, you pay back in distance. A 5:1 block and tackle needing 1/5 the force means pulling 5 times the length of rope through your hands.

Real block-and-tackle systems lose some of this advantage to friction in the pulleys - the more pulleys/wraps, the more friction loss, which is why very high-ratio systems are less efficient in practice than the simple math suggests.

diagram.alt: A sailor pulling a rope through a block-and-tackle pulley system to lift a heavy crate
diagram.caption: Figure 7-5. A block and tackle makes work easier - five rope segments supporting the load give a mechanical advantage of about 5.

title: Fastener Basics: Screws, Bolts & Nuts
summary: "Screw" and "bolt" aren't interchangeable - the difference is how the fastener is meant to be tightened.
quick_actions: A bolt is designed to be tightened by turning a nut (or a tapped hole) while the bolt head itself doesn't rotate - torque is applied at the nut end.

A screw is designed to be tightened by turning the fastener's own head, cutting or engaging threads directly in the material it's driven into (wood screws, sheet-metal screws) or into a pre-tapped hole (machine screws).

Thread pitch is the distance between adjacent threads - a coarser (bigger) pitch drives in faster and resists stripping in soft materials; a finer pitch holds more tightly and resists loosening under vibration.

Matching threads matters more than matching size alone: a fastener with the right diameter but the wrong thread pitch or standard (e.g. metric vs. inch, or a fine vs. coarse series at the same diameter) will not thread in correctly, even if it starts to catch.

Common head-drive types (slotted, Phillips, hex/Allen, Torx) each need their own matching driver - forcing the wrong driver into a head is one of the most common ways to strip a fastener before it's even fully seated.
more_info: Locking methods (lock washers, nylon-insert lock nuts, thread-locking compound, cotter pins on castellated nuts) exist because plain threads can back themselves loose under vibration - choosing one is about matching the locking method to how much vibration/reuse the joint will actually see, not just picking whichever is on hand.

title: Torque Concepts
summary: Torque is a twisting force applied at a distance - and "tight enough" has a real upper limit, not just a lower one.
quick_actions: Torque = force x distance from the pivot (the fastener's center). A longer wrench handle gives more torque for the same hand force - which is exactly why "cheater bars" on a wrench are risky: they can easily exceed what a fastener or the material around it can safely take.

Under-tightening a fastener risks it loosening under vibration or load; over-tightening risks stripping the threads, snapping the fastener, or crushing/damaging whatever it's clamping - both directions are real failure modes, not just the obvious one.

A torque wrench measures and limits how much torque you actually apply, instead of relying on "feel" - genuinely important on anything with a manufacturer-specified torque value (engine/mechanical components, wheel lug nuts, anything structural).

Torque specifications assume specific conditions (clean/dry threads unless "lubricated" is specified, a specific thread condition) - the same torque wrench reading can clamp very differently on a dry vs. an oiled thread, which is why torque specs and lubrication instructions are always given together, not separately.

When no torque spec is available: snug plus a modest additional turn is a reasonable default for small fasteners in non-critical applications - but there is no substitute for a real spec on anything safety-critical or structural.
more_info: This is a concept overview, not a substitute for a manufacturer's actual torque specification table - always use the specified value and lubrication condition for anything where getting it wrong has real consequences.

title: Bearings & Lubrication
summary: A bearing's whole job is turning sliding friction into much lower rolling friction - and it fails when that stops happening.
quick_actions: A plain (sleeve/bushing) bearing is just a low-friction surface a shaft slides against - simple and cheap, but higher friction than a rolling-element bearing and more dependent on adequate lubrication to avoid direct metal-to-metal contact.

A ball or roller bearing replaces sliding friction with rolling friction using hardened balls or rollers between an inner and outer race - lower friction and less heat than a plain bearing under the same load, but more sensitive to contamination (dirt/grit) and to being overloaded sideways (radially) versus along its axis, depending on the bearing type.

Lubricant does three jobs at once: reduces friction between moving surfaces, carries heat away from the contact point, and helps flush out or suspend small contamination particles rather than letting them grind into the surfaces.

Grease vs. oil: grease stays in place (good for a bearing that's hard to reseal or re-lubricate often), while oil flows and can be filtered/circulated/cooled - the right choice depends on the mechanism's own design, not a general rule that one is always better.

Warning signs of bearing trouble: unusual noise (grinding, squealing), noticeable heat, visible play/wobble in a shaft that should be firm, or discolored/gritty-feeling lubricant - any of these is worth investigating before the bearing fails completely, since a bearing that's already making noise is usually well past the point of simple relubrication fixing it.
more_info: Using the wrong grease/oil type (or none at all) is one of the most common causes of premature mechanical failure in field equipment - when in doubt, the equipment's own manual and its specified lubricant type take priority over a generic substitute.

title: Common Hand Tools: Choosing the Right One
summary: Most hand-tool damage and injuries come from using the almost-right tool instead of stopping to find the right one.
quick_actions: Screwdrivers: match both the drive type (slotted, Phillips, etc.) and the size - a too-small driver in a screw head is a common cause of stripping it, and a too-large one can damage the surrounding material.

Wrenches: a properly-fitting wrench (correct size, fully seated on the fastener) distributes force across the full flat of a bolt/nut; a loose or mis-sized wrench concentrates force on the corners and rounds them off - after which every other tool has a harder time gripping it too.

Pliers are for gripping and bending, not for turning fasteners in place of a wrench - pliers' serrated jaws chew up a fastener's corners quickly, which is exactly the damage that then makes the fastener need pliers again next time.

Never use a wrench, screwdriver, or any hand tool as a hammer, pry bar, or chisel unless it's specifically designed for that (some screwdrivers are rated for light prying; most are not) - tools used outside their design intent are a common source of both tool breakage and injury.

A damaged tool (mushroomed chisel/punch head, bent screwdriver tip, cracked handle) should be repaired or replaced before its next use, not "used carefully" - tool failure under force is unpredictable and often throws debris.
more_info: The full Tools and Their Uses manual in the Document Library below covers the complete range of hand tools (levels, squares, gages, vises, clamps, pliers/tongs, screwdrivers, wrenches) in far more depth than this overview attempts.

title: Mechanical Measurement: Calipers & Micrometers
summary: A steel rule measures to about 1/64 inch by eye; calipers and micrometers measure far more precisely than that.
quick_actions: Slide calipers give a quick outside or inside measurement read directly off a sliding scale - fast, but limited to the precision you can read by eye off that scale (typically to about 1/64 inch or 0.5mm).

Vernier calipers add a second, finer sliding scale (the vernier) that lets you read much more precisely than a plain scale alone - typically to 0.001 inch or 0.02mm - by finding which vernier line most closely aligns with a main-scale line.

A micrometer uses a precisely-machined screw thread (commonly 40 threads per inch) so that one full turn of the thimble corresponds to an exact, known linear distance - this lets it measure even more precisely than a vernier caliper, typically to 0.001 inch or better.

"Outside" measurements (across the outside of an object) and "inside" measurements (across an internal bore or gap) need the tool's outside jaws/anvils or inside jaws/rods respectively - the same instrument often does both, but not with the same set of jaws.

Zero the tool (check that fully closed jaws read exactly zero) before trusting a precision measurement - a caliper or micrometer that doesn't zero correctly will be consistently off by that same error on every reading until it's corrected or accounted for.

title: A Practical Approach to Mechanical Troubleshooting
summary: Find out what actually changed before you start taking things apart.
quick_actions: Start with what's different: what changed right before the problem started (a new noise, a recent repair, a specific event)? A problem that appeared suddenly usually has a specific, findable cause; one that's developed gradually usually points to wear or a slowly-worsening condition instead.

Check the simple, likely things before the complex, unlikely ones: a loose connection, an empty tank, a tripped breaker, or a disconnected linkage account for a large share of real-world mechanical problems and take seconds to rule out.

Isolate before you disassemble: can you narrow the problem to one system or component through observation/testing, rather than opening up everything that could conceivably be involved? Unnecessary disassembly adds new opportunities for something to go back together wrong.

Keep track of what you remove and in what order, especially fasteners of different lengths/threads from different locations - a phone photo before disassembly, or a simple sketch, is often faster than trying to remember afterward.

Know when to stop: a repair that requires specialized tools, parts, or safety equipment you don't have, or that involves a system where a mistake is genuinely dangerous (pressurized systems, electrical mains, structural load-bearing components), is a stopping point, not a challenge to push through.
more_info: This is a general problem-solving approach, not a substitute for a specific piece of equipment's own service manual - when one exists and is available, it takes priority over general troubleshooting principles.
